body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Family meetings before hospital discharge and 30-day readmission in adults aged 75 and over: a matched comparison in two hospitals","authors":"Adebayo-Stroud K, Lindgren-Mwale P, Hartigan-Oyelowo S","year":2021,"venue":"Journal of Hospital Social Work Practice","doi":"10.5555/jhswp.2021.0233","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared 612 patients aged 75 and over who had a documented family discharge meeting with 1,224 patients without a meeting, matched on age, ward and discharge month, in two general hospitals. Thirty-day readmission was 17.8 percent with a meeting and 18.4 percent without. When the analysis was restricted to meetings that a family member attended and that produced a written plan, readmission was 13.1 percent against 18.4 percent. Meetings were more often held for patients with previous admissions and for patients living alone. The authors note that booked meetings and attended meetings are different exposures and that residual confounding by case complexity is likely."},{"title":"Confounding by case complexity in evaluations of discharge planning: a methods commentary with a worked example","authors":"Pellegrini-Achterberg D, Osei-Wakefield R","year":2018,"venue":"Care Transitions Methods Notes","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Patients chosen for enhanced discharge planning usually carry a higher baseline risk of readmission than those who are not, so crude comparisons can make an effective service look harmful. In a worked example from one hospital, the crude odds ratio of 1.35 became 0.82 after adjustment for prior admissions, frailty and living alone. We recommend defining the exposure precisely, measuring the complexity that drives selection before discharge, matching or adjusting on it, and reporting how estimates change as each confounder is added. Unmeasured complexity, such as family conflict, cannot be removed by adjustment and should be discussed openly."},{"title":"Structured family involvement in discharge planning for older inpatients: a systematic review of sixteen studies","authors":"Moreno-Blackwood T, Uchenna-Falk L, Sorensen-Iqbal A","year":2023,"venue":"Transitions of Care Review","doi":"10.5555/tcr.2023.0118","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We searched five databases to 2022 for studies of structured family involvement in hospital discharge planning for adults aged 65 and over. Sixteen studies met the inclusion criteria: five randomised trials and eleven observational studies. In the trials, structured family involvement reduced 30-day readmission (pooled risk ratio 0.84, 95 percent CI 0.71 to 0.99). Observational studies were inconsistent, and those that did not adjust for complexity tended to show higher readmission with family involvement. Definitions of family involvement ranged from a single telephone call to a structured meeting with a written plan, and no study reported carers' own outcomes."},{"title":"Sampling controls from the discharge population and reading exposure from clinical notes in readmission studies","authors":"Kagame-Whitfield B, Lorenzen-Abara M","year":2020,"venue":"Morrowvale Health Services Epidemiology","doi":"10.5555/jhse.2020.0047","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Readmission studies often need exposure details that exist only in free-text notes. Using a completed study in one hospital, we compared reading notes for every discharge with reading notes only for readmitted patients and a random sample of patients who were not readmitted. Sampling controls at a ratio of two per case reduced note reading by about 80 percent compared with reviewing every discharge, and the odds ratio for the exposure changed by less than 5 percent. Agreement between two readers on whether a family member attended a discharge meeting was good (kappa 0.81). Readers who knew the patient's readmission status coded borderline notes differently."},{"title":"Family conferences on medical wards: regional service evaluation summary","authors":"Regional Health Authority Older People's Services Team","year":null,"venue":"Regional Health Authority service evaluation series","providerType":"report","abstract":"This summary describes family conferences held on the medical wards of three hospitals in the region. Conferences brought together the patient, family members, ward staff and a social worker before discharge. Across the three hospitals, 1,140 conferences were held during the evaluation period, and staff surveyed afterwards said conferences improved communication with families. Families were not asked for their views. The summary lists the number of conferences by hospital and month and gives examples of plans agreed. It does not describe how patients were chosen for a conference, what happened after discharge, or when the evaluation period began and ended."},{"title":"Carers' experience of discharge planning meetings for older relatives: a qualitative study","authors":"Fairweather-Nnamdi C, Holm-Estrada J","year":2022,"venue":"Brackenmoor Journal of Family Caregiving","doi":"10.5555/jfcr.2022.0309","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We interviewed 28 carers of older relatives discharged from two hospitals about discharge planning meetings. Carers valued meetings that were booked with notice and that ended with a written plan naming who to call. Many working carers could not attend weekday daytime meetings, and carers without a car found the hospital hard to reach; several said they only heard about a meeting after it had happened. Joining by telephone helped some carers but made it harder to ask questions. Carers described being expected to take on care they had not agreed to. The authors conclude that access to meetings is unequal among families."},{"title":"Pre-discharge family meetings and early readmission among frail older adults: conference abstract","authors":"Varga-Oduya E, Chen-Macallister R","year":null,"venue":"Society for Transitional Care annual meeting abstract book","providerType":"conference-abstract","abstract":"Background: family meetings before discharge are thought to prevent early readmission. Methods: adults discharged from a teaching hospital were grouped by whether a family meeting was held before discharge. Results: of 140 patients, those with a meeting were readmitted within 30 days less often than those without (12 against 21 percent, p equal to 0.09). Conclusions: family meetings may reduce early readmission and a larger study is planned. The abstract does not state how patients were selected for meetings, the age range, whether the groups were comparable, or whether any adjustment was made, and the listing gives no year of presentation."}]}
